A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RedDebate. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original HarmBench and CoSafe experiments, memory and debate ablations, TriviaQA evaluations, and validation against human safety annotations.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark-transfer, frontier-model, over-refusal, retrieval, baseline, and efficiency experiments.

M1.justification: Section 5.3 introduces an optional early-stopping variant that terminates debate when all agents produce safe responses in a round. The three principal debate strategies, four memory configurations, core algorithms, and agent prompts otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendices C.3 and C.6 add Aegis-2, WildJailbreak, and XSTest, covering broader safety categories, diverse jailbreak prompts, and safe requests resembling unsafe ones. They also test memory transfer to unseen benchmarks. HarmBench, CoSafe, and TriviaQA are retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds unguided Self-Revision to the HarmBench/CoSafe comparisons in Tables 1–2 and Best-of-N independent sampling to the HarmBench comparison in Table 3. Standard Prompting and constitution-guided Self-Critique remain. These additions substantially strengthen controls for isolated revision and additional sampling.

E3.justification: Added protocols include Best-of-N with N=3 and 5 and best/average/worst aggregation, single-round memory-transfer tests, a frontier-scale PReD triad, and replacement of the Socratic guide. v3 also adds retrieval evaluation at K=5/10 and one- and two-round conditions to the existing round-count ablation.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of memory transfer, frontier-scale generalization, Socratic-guide dependence, targeted over-refusal, retrieval reliability, wall-clock costs, and early stopping. It extends the round-count ablation and adds a conservative-agent case study in Figure 14. Earlier evaluator, instruction-tuning, diversity, and agent-count analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing 2,104 ± 228 token-usage summary is unchanged; new result tables do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include Qwen's WildJailbreak error rates of 41.5% without memory and 6.5% with transferred HarmBench TLTM (v3 Table 6), and hybrid-memory XSTest compliance losses of 14 and 8 points for Mistral and Phi (Table 10). Retained CoSafe totals also change: Standard Prompting for the second triad rises from 7.9% to 8.1% in Table 1, and first-triad SReD with Unified memory changes from 2.4% to 2.5% in Table 2.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(5), including the ER and AGR definitions, are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the added metric descriptions and mechanism discussions do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion newly position RedDebate explicitly as an inference-time complement to existing safety alignment. The central automated debate-and-memory contribution and headline HarmBench reduction claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications concerning untested memory poisoning, disabled reasoning mode, hybrid-memory over-refusal, weaker Socratic guides losing context, and early stopping sacrificing useful feedback. It also interprets cumulative adapter training as mitigating forgetting and semantically similar retrievals as cushioning retrieval misses. These considerably expand the applicability and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses four 80GB A100 GPUs, disabled thinking/reasoning mode, and detailed inference-time and Socratic-agent overhead information. Disabled reasoning is newly documented, not an established change from v2. Existing LoRA settings, prompt templates, memory implementation details, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands discussion of training-time alignment, distribution shift, reward hacking, and alignment faking, adding works such as Ouyang et al. (2022), Casper et al. (2023b), and Greenblatt et al. (2024). Section 5.1 explains the complementary positioning and exclusion of training-based comparators. New benchmark, model, sampling, and guardrail references further broaden the literature coverage.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. v3 revises the introduction and Self-Critique explanation, standardizes abbreviations, collects cost discussion into Section 5.3, moves limitations into Appendix A, and removes the separate LLM-use statement. These are localized narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: v3 converts the main text and references to two columns, redraws framework Figures 1–2, and revises the vulnerability figure's labels and caption. It adds seven tables and Figure 14, expands existing comparison and round-ablation tables, and redistributes retained appendix figures and prompt displays.

improvement.justification: Beyond v2's Self-Critique and token-budget comparisons, v3 adds controls for unguided revision and independent sampling, tests unseen-benchmark transfer, and directly examines over-refusal and guide dependence. These address important gaps in the evidence for interaction benefits and generalization. Some broad prose still overstates the findings, especially helpfulness despite hybrid-memory compliance losses in Table 10, but the stronger controls and newly exposed limitations substantially improve the paper's overall evidential quality.
